paper_title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Many uses of language model end in decision from closed set: which tool to call, whether retrieved passage supports claim, which intent message expresses, which of four answers is right. In established terms these are zero-shot classification and multiple-choice problems whose label set changes from instance to instance. Current practice answers them in one of three ways. large language model (LLM) can be prompted and its output parsed, which is slow and sensitive to the order in which the options are listed [1, 2]. natural language inference (NLI) model can score each candidate label as hypothesis [3, 4], which needs one forward pass per option. Or classifier can be fine-tuned for each task, which does not transfer to new label sets. recent request format, introduced with the Jev decision model [5] and formalised by later work [6,7], packages such problems as typed decisions: structured request (a state plus typed questions) goes in, and probability for every allowed option comes out, with no generated text  (Fig. 2)  . Because the output space is fixed, model for such decisions can in principle be small. This paper asks two questions: how small an encoder can be, and how it should read the options. The second question has two classical answers. Per-option scoring, as in BERTs multiple-choice head [8, 9] and in NLI zero-shot classification, encodes the context once per option and normalises the scores across options; joint scoring encodes the context with all options in one sequence and reads one score per option from marker tokens, as in UniMC [10] and, for typed decisions, Dinah-0 [11]. Joint scoring costs one pass per question instead of n, which is why recent compact decision models use it, but the two have not been compared under controlled conditions for this kind of decision. We train Crivo, family of six joint encoders from 17M to 1B parameters fine-tuned from the Ettin rerankers [12, 13] with an [OPT] readout adapted from Dinah-0, and we run three-seed controlled grid at 32M that compares joint and per-option reading with everything else fixed, from two initialisations. The grid is scored on held-out sample of the 37benchmark public suite of the Decision Index [14] (hereafter, the board), public leaderboard for this format (public-suite skill). We evaluate the family on two public external benchmarks audited for overlap with our training data, System1Arena (S1-Arena) [15] for typed decisions and BTZSC [16] for zero-shot text classification, against named baselines run under one protocol, and we measure option-order robustness, calibration and latency on stated hardware. As supporting evidence we report the boards private tests, whose official score comes only from tests its maintainers run, together with Prumo, rule engine with no learned parameters that shows what those tests reward without learning. Fig. 1 summarises the external and the private-test results.

sections.title: 2.1 Option scoring: per-option, joint and list-
sections.content: wise How an encoder should read set of candidate answers is an old question, and the reader study of Section 5 belongs to it. Per-option scoring encodes the context once per option and normalises the scores across options. It is the standard multiple-choice head of BERT-style encoders on SWAG and RACE [8,9,17], the basis of zero-shot classification by entailment, which scores each label as an NLI hypothesis [3] using models trained on corpora such as MNLI [18] (BART-largeMNLI [19] and the DeBERTa-v3 [20] classifiers of Laurer et al. [4, 21] are the standard checkpoints), and of label-pair classifiers such as TARS [22]. Its cost grows with the number of options, and options cannot be compared directly, which multiple-choice reading-comprehension models address with option-comparison and co-matching layers [23, 24]. 2 Joint scoring puts the context and all options in one sequence and reads one score per option. UniMC [10], extended in IEEE Access [25], recasts natural language understanding tasks as multiple choice: an option-mask token precedes every option, each predicts yes through the maskedlanguage-model head, and the yes logits are normalised across options; an attention mask keeps the options from attending to each other, so all options are read in one pass but scored without direct comparison. GLiNER [26] prepends one marker per entity type and reads all types in one pass; GLiClass [27] applies the same idea to zero-shot sequence classification, encoding text with all its candidate labels, which attend to each other and to the text, and reports several times the throughput of pairwise NLI cross-encoders; and LACO [28] jointly encodes document with all labels of fixed label set for supervised multi-label classification. Recasting classification as multiple choice over category labels has also been studied in IEEE Access [29]. In retrieval, listwise cross-encoders such as Set-Encoder [30] let candidates attend to each other and make the result invariant to their order. For LLMs, multiple-choice answers are usually read from the logit of the option letter [31], which is sensitive to option order [1, 2]. BTZSC compares crossencoders, embedding models, rerankers and LLMs under one zero-shot protocol [16]. Crivos released reader is joint reader in the UniMC line, adapted to typed decisions through Dinah-0. Unlike UniMC, and like GLiClass, it lets the options attend to each other; it also uses fresh head on reranker backbone and is trained on typed decisions rather than on converted multiple-choice datasets. Our reader study compares it with per-option scoring under controlled conditions (Section 5).

sections.title: 2.2 Typed decision models
sections.content: Jev introduced the request format used here, under the name System One, together with hosted decision model [5]. Independent evaluations and an early evidence review followed within weeks [3235], among them S1-Arena, typeddecision benchmark built from 268 public sources with public leaderboard [15], and harness in which fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-large wins on almost every labelled benchmark [36]. Most open decision models are decoders read through option letters or deliberation [3740]. Encoder approaches are closer to ours. Decision models have been built from biomedical sentence encoders [41]; Bekko released large training set and 17M400M models on the same Ettin rerankers that we start from [42, 43]; Laya, 421M ModernBERT-based model, was independently reproduced and found under-confident [44]; Verdict answers all questions of request in one pass under structured attention mask [45]; and Narrow Decision Models and Jeva formalise the interface with bidirectional encoder and structural requirements such as permutation invariance [6,7]. The [OPT] readout that Crivo uses comes from the Dinah-0 model [11], 150M encoder for this format whose option markers resemble UniMCs.

sections.title: 2.3 Cross-encoders, compact encoders and
sections.content: distillation Crivo is cross-encoder in the sense of monoBERT [46], as opposed to the siamese bi-encoders of Sentence-BERT [47]: the context and the candidates are encoded jointly. Its backbones are the reranker fine-tunes [13] of the Ettin encoders [12], which follow ModernBERT [48], successor of BERT [8]. Smaller family members are distilled from larger ones, as compact encoders often are: with soft targets [49] as in DistilBERT [50], by attention distillation as in MiniLM [51], and in recent task-aware distillation into encoders [52].

sections.title: 2.4 Calibration and selective prediction
sections.content: We report expected calibration error [53, 54], the Brier score [55] and selective-prediction risk [56]. Pre-trained transformers are reasonably calibrated in domain and less so out of domain [57]; decision models have been found over-confident when answers need specialist knowledge [33] and underconfident in the case of Laya [44].

sections.title: 2.5 Leaderboards, holdout reuse and contam-
sections.content: ination Reusing test set for selection overfits it [58], models lose accuracy on fresh test sets built to replicate the original distribution [59], and leaderboards can be distorted when some providers test many private variants and publish only the best [60]; contamination audits [61] are one response. Our negative result (Section 7.3) is case where the proxy that failed was our own development panel, not the public test set. Following Schwartz et al. [62], we report quality against cost.

sections.title: 2.6 Rule-based and parameter-free baselines
sections.content: Parameter-free classifiers such as compression with nearest neighbours [63] and deterministic tiers that hand over to model only when needed [64] show that simple baselines can be strong and diagnostic. Prumo follows this line: fixed pipeline of classical components (BM25 [65], code execution, game-tree search, truth tables, calendar arithmetic) used as diagnostic of what decision benchmark rewards without learning.

sections.title: 3.2 External benchmarks
sections.content: System1-Arena (S1-Arena) [15] is typed-decision benchmark in the same request format, with open data and code and public leaderboard. We use the 13 non-agentic domains of its public snapshot, which its overall leaderboard score averages: 41,183 requests, 72,817 questions and 209 tasks (the published leaderboard also includes 2,043 requests that can only be built locally, so its rows are not on exactly our item set). We map binary questions to binary predicates; nothing else is changed. The statistic is the benchmarks own: pertask accuracy averaged over tasks, computed with its scorer (unanswered counts as wrong). Every Crivo leaves 72 questions unanswered: they belong to 24 requests longer than the 32,768 tokens that the released engine reads, which it declines rather than truncates. BTZSC [16] is zero-shot text classification benchmark of 22 datasets in sentiment, emotion, intent and topic, with published results for NLI cross-encoders, rerankers, embedding models and LLMs. We render each item as one multiplechoice question whose options are BTZSCs own label verbalisations, with one fixed instruction chosen before any 4 plus option, softmax of the entailment logits over options. As in BTZSCs harness, the premise is truncated at 512 tokens (1,024 for BART). Small LLMs with letter readout: Qwen3-0.6B [67] and Gemma-3-1B-it [68]; next-token probabilities of the option letters, renormalised, with BTZSCs prompt generalised to question. Both run without chat template or permutation debiasing [1]; they measure plain letter readout, not the best these models can do (Gemma-31B-it is close to the uniform guess on S1-Arena). The untrained Ettin-32M reranker, i.e. Crivo-32M before training, scoring each option as document. uniform guess. Inputs baseline cannot process (too long or too many options) count as wrong, as in the Decision Index. We also cite the published S1-Arena and BTZSC rows, which come from the benchmarks own harnesses and carry no paired intervals. We did not run the compact decision encoders of other authors (Bekko, Dinah-1, the tasksource decider, Mola) or GLiClass [27] on the external benchmarks, and none of them publishes results on S1-Arena or BTZSC that we could compare with; they appear only on the Decision Index.

sections.title: 3.5 The Decision Index public suite
sections.content: The Decision Index [14, 69] is public leaderboard for this format. Entrants run public suite of 37 benchmarks in five areas (knowledge and reasoning, language understanding, retrieval and classification, tools and automation, arts and taste) with the open kit and submit their outputs. Each benchmark is chance-corrected, (s c)/(1 c) clipped to [0, 1], and the public index is 100 times the weighted mean. The suite covers tool use [7073], intent classification [74, 75], fact verification [76, 77], NLI [7880], sentiment and stance [8184], commonsense and knowledge [8589], reasoning and code [9095], retrieval [96, 97], and arts and taste [98101]. The boards official ranking uses only private tests run by its maintainers (Section 7).

sections.title: 3.6 Statistics
sections.content: For S1-Arena and BTZSC we use per-item paired bootstrap: requests are resampled with replacement inside each task or dataset (the questions of request move together), the official statistic is recomputed, and the same draws serve all systems (B = 2,000). This interval is conditional on the benchmarks tasks. second, wider interval resamples tasks within domains (S1-Arena) or datasets (BTZSC) and speaks to tasks like these. For the twelve comparisons of the six Crivo models with DeBERTa (all and unseen tasks) we also give Holm-adjusted bootstrap p-values. The ablation grid uses Welch 95% intervals over three seeds per arm; with 3 against 3 seeds they have 24 degrees of freedom and assume normality, and an exact permutation test could not go below = 0.10, so we treat intervals that barely exclude zero as suggestive. Correlations across board entries use bootstrap over entries (B = 10,000); entries are not independent (several are fine-tunes of one base), and we did not cluster the bootstrap. Tables and text give accuracy, skill and their differences as fractions; where we speak of points (abstract, introduction) point is 0.01 of such fraction, while board scores are on 0100 scale.

sections.title: 3.7 Robustness and latency measurement
sections.content: Option-order robustness uses 3,841 multiple-choice questions (2,833 requests) sampled from the public suite: each is answered under three random permutations and under reversed order, and 258 binary requests are also answered with their two options swapped. We report the share of questions whose chosen option changes; requests system cannot process (121 for DeBERTa, 200 for the two LLMs) are excluded. Latency is measured one request at time on the first 1,000 requests of seeded shuffle of this sample, the same for every system: on one unshared NVIDIA A100-SXM4 40 GB (bf16 autocast, 20 warm-up requests), and on 16 threads of an AMD EPYC 7J13 with nothing else running (fp32, 10 warm-up requests, first 80 requests, all answered by every system). Each request is timed once, except in paired GPU run of the peroption checkpoint (Section 5) and Crivo-32M, whose two alternating passes are averaged. Crivo batches up to 32 questions of request per call, the NLI baseline up to 32 premise hypothesis pairs, and the per-option reader all options of request in shared batches. On the GPU, requests system cannot process are not timed (40 of 1,000 for DeBERTa, which flatters it).

sections.title: 4.3 Training data
sections.content: The training mix has 638,306 questions in stage 1, 169,437 in stage 2 and 24,635 in stage 3. It combines the Bekko System One data [42] (at most 1,200 rows per subset), 328 tasksource families [102,103] (40 further families held out entirely), procedural typed decisions [104, 105], code-generated decision families with exact labels (policies with exceptions, opaque label rules, schedules, ordinal severity, dates, propositional logic, executed code), synthetic tool-use dialogues built from public function-calling data, and the train splits of the public suites source datasets, capped at 5,000 rows per source, about half rewritten into other request layouts. No outputs of Jev or of other proprietary decision APIs were used as targets. The API-Bank [72] train split repeats dialogues of the boards test pool; it is excluded from the released recipe but was in the training data of Crivo-150M v1, the teacher of Crivo-17M.

sections.content: All models start from the Ettin reranker of the same size (cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-*-v1) [13]; Table 2 lists them. The six released models share the recipe below. Two models trained with an earlier recipe, Crivo-150M v1 and Crivo-32M v1, appear only as the teacher of Crivo17M (Crivo-150M v1) and in the recipe comparison of Section 7.3; unmarked names refer to the released models.

sections.title: 4.5 Prumo: a floor with no learned parameters
sections.content: Prumo reads the same requests and returns the same typed answers, but contains no model, no embeddings and no corpus statistics. Each question passes through twelve capabilities in fixed order: sandboxed code execution, chess search (alphabeta, 7,000 nodes), BM25 tool relevance with schema validation, BM25 retrieval, lexical grounding, consensus 6 centroid, IDF label overlap, chord templates, exact Boolean logic and SAT, exhaustive puzzle search (claimed only if the solution is unique), calendar arithmetic, and exact-fraction arithmetic. capability either claims the question and returns probabilities or passes it on; unclaimed questions get the uniform distribution, so their expected score is exactly chance. The engine never reads benchmark names or item ids. It is about 2.7k lines of Python with one dependency (python-chess); its only numbers are 527 hand-set constants, 454 of them chess piece-square values. Thresholds were chosen on train and development splits. All budgets are counted in operations, so outputs are bit-identical across machines. Prumo executes code taken from requests in sandbox with resource limits and should not be exposed to untrusted input without further isolation.

sections.title: 5.1 Design
sections.content: Joint versus PerJoint reading lets options attend to each other in one pass, which could help comparison; per-option reading re-reads the context for every option but matches the (query, document) format on which cross-encoder rerankers are trained. sections.title: 5.3 Cost
sections.content: Per request, the per-option reader needs 5.2 times more forward sequences on pub15, 6.4 times on S1-60 and 13.1 times on BTZSC-500, because it re-encodes the state once per option. We timed the per-option checkpoint (seed 0) against the released joint Crivo-32M, which has the same architecture, on the same requests (Table 7, paired block). On the A100, over 1,000 requests in two alternating passes, the medians are the same (10.7 against 10.4 ms), but the mean is 4.3 times higher (59.0 against 13.7 ms) and the 95th percentile 10 times. On 16 CPU threads the median request takes 41.0 against 21.9 ms (1.9 times), the mean 3,728 against 139 ms (27 times) and the 95th percentile 32 times longer. Typical requests are cheap either way; the cost falls on long requests with many options. Per-option training with the full recipe would cost about 3.84.2 times the joint readers tokens on the main stages and 23 times on the long-input stage (catalogues of about 44 tools share one state). The choice is therefore trade-off. Where many options or questions share one long state (tool catalogues, intent lists with 77151 labels), the joint reader is far cheaper. Where reranker checkpoint is available and mean and tail latency are acceptable, the per-option reader is more accurate, even at approximately matched training compute. From raw encoder, per-option reading bought no accuracy in our runs.

sections.content: Table 6 collects the boards calibration measurement (maintainer-computed on 1-in-6 request sample) and ours on the external benchmarks (expected calibration error with 10 equal-mass bins, ECE, averaged with equal weight per task or dataset; and the multi-class Brier score). Crivos calibration depends on whether it has seen the source corpora: its ECE is lowest where most datasets were seen in training, and it is over-confident on unseen tasks. On all 22 BTZSC datasets, 18 of them seen in training, every Crivo has lower ECE than every baseline (item intervals exclude zero); on the four unseen datasets this no longer holds: Qwen3-0.6B has lower ECE than Crivo-68M and Crivo-150M, and DeBERTa than Crivo-150M. On S1Arena, Crivo-17M has lower ECE than DeBERTa (0.021 [0.027, 0.015]) and every Crivo lower ECE than the two LLMs, but ECE does not fall with size and the larger Crivos are worse than DeBERTa. sections.title: 7.4 What a rule engine reveals about the board
sections.content: With no learned parameters, Prumo scores Full of 12.21 on the private tests (S = 15.78, = 5.60), above Crivo17M (11.11) and both Bekko models at 17M and 68M (5.72, 9.99), and below Crivo-32M (13.70). On the same skills it ties Crivo-17M (15.78 against 15.88), and on new domains it is above every Crivo below 400M, probably because some new-domain tasks contain structures it solves exactly. On the external benchmarks it is near chance (S1-Arena 0.340, BTZSC 0.209). The natural reading is that part of the board rewards format-specific solving, which hand-written engine can do without any notion of the task; this weakens the board as evidence for the encoders, and is why we place it after the external benchmarks. Its board ECE (0.047) is low mostly because unclaimed questions receive uniform answers. Because Prumo learns nothing, its publicprivate gap on benchmark measures how well hand-written capability transfers to fresh items of the same skill (Fig. 8; = 0.77 over 34 benchmarks): lexical capabilities hold (tool retrieval 0.39 public, 0.51 private), exact solvers do not (CRUXEval 0.997, 0.28; BBH 0.47, 0.07), presumably because parser exact on the public format stops firing on another presentation.

sections.title: 10 Conclusion
sections.content: Joint or per-option? At 32M and matched compute, the answer depends on the starting checkpoint. From crossencoder reranker, whose pair input matches per-option reading, scoring each option separately is more accurate (+0.028 public-suite skill, with the same sign on two external benchmarks but not significantly on their unseen tasks); from the raw encoder, the cheaper joint reader is as good. Per-option scoring costs 513 times the encoder passes, little at the median and much in the tail, so the reader should follow the applications latency budget. How small? Joint encoders from 68M up beat 435M zero-shot NLI classifier on all tasks of an overlap-audited typed-decision benchmark, models up to 150M are at least on par with it on unseen tasks, and the 17M model answers median request in about 14 ms on CPU. For benchmark maintainers, parameter-free engine that matches 17M model on same-skill private tests is cheap probe for format-specific shortcuts. Reader study. The S1-Arena audit is nameand string-based, and only four BTZSC datasets are unseen. The comparison is with generic NLI classifiers and small LLMs, not the closest same-interface encoders (Section 3.4), and it mixes backbone, readout and training data; only the readout is isolated. Board, baselines and latency. Private scores come from one run of each model on tests we cannot inspect. We did not fine-tune DeBERTa-v3-large per task, the supervised ceiling reported elsewhere [36]. Latency has no batched throughput or operation counts, and the 80-request CPU sample makes means sensitive to few long requests. Use and scope. The models are over-confident on new tasks, so thresholds for routing actions must be set on the target task; in hand-coded sample of 70 Crivo-68M errors on the public suite, the most confident errors were wrong tool or action selections. They do not replace supervised intask training or large models on knowledge-heavy and newdomain decisions. Training and evaluation are in English only.
